agent_notes: The superscription is verse 1 in the Hebrew (KJV 48:0). The lamed in livnei Korach can mean 'for', 'of' or 'by'; the literal layer keeps the neutral 'to/for' and the commentary names the options.

dimminu: STEPBible 'reflected on'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read 'we waited/hoped' (cf. Ps 37:7 dom), Rashi also cites Menachem for 'thought' (Esth 4:13). I kept 'we have pondered' with the double sense noted.

Right hand is the grammatical subject, as requested: מָלְאָה is feminine, agreeing with יְמִינֶךָ (feminine) and not with צֶדֶק (masculine). That is why YLT's 'righteousness hath filled thy right hand' is less likely. I read צֶדֶק as adverbial or accusative of fullness, '[with] righteousness'. Meiri takes צדק as 'uprightness' (cf. Deut 16:20); Metzudat David as power that does not come by violence.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses סֹבּוּ as 'go around' and הַקִּיפוּהָ as 'and go round it'. Both are kept; the two verbs are near-synonyms (sabab and naqaf) and I kept the pair visible in English as 'circle' and 'go around' rather than collapsing them.

פַּסְּגוּ is a hapax. The STEPBible gloss 'walk through' follows the lemma פָּסַג; I glossed it 'pass through' (literal) and mention Rashi and Radak's link to פִּסְגָּה 'summit' (Deut 3:17, 27), which gives 'go up to the heights of'. Radak and Ibn Ezra take it as 'look at, see as a peak'. My dramatic layer uses 'climb among' because that keeps both senses. The sense of חֵיל as the low outer wall is from Radak and Metzudat Zion (citing Lam 2:8); I corrected the STEPBible gloss 'rampart' only by adding 'outer'.
In the packet's Targum the verse is rendered with 'its inhabitants' and 'its palaces' glossed as buildings; I did not use it as a source for any claim, only the named medieval commentators.

Revised after the reviewer's request. Attribution now follows the packet: Ibn Ezra reports that the Masorete reads two words ('until our death'), while the one-word 'almut' is the reading of the other commentators. 'Forever' is credited to Menachem (cited by Rashi), Metzudat Zion and Malbim. Radak gives both readings, 'until our death' first. Ibn Ezra's own first gloss is 'like olamit', so he also lists the one-word reading before the Masorete's.

The five English versions agree on 'even unto death' except BBE, which drops the phrase, and YLT, which has 'over death'. I kept the two-word Hebrew as written in the text (al-mut) in the literal layer and in the glosses, and gave the one-word reading in the commentary. The Targum's 'like the days of our youth' is a third reading (from 'alumim'), and I mention it without taking it up. The Meiri passage on the 'after death' reading is not cited in the note, because I could not reconcile its wording with the other readings.
